---
title: "Research"
---

The question that ties my research together is how we measure what exercise does to the body and what we can claim from what we have measured. Three research lines follow from it. They do not carry the same weight or belong to the same stage of my career, but they share the same question: how the body adapts, how we measure that adaptation, and how it responds acutely to exercise.

## How the body adapts

My main current research line focuses on strength and muscle mechanics. It is organised around EXCURSE—*Muscle Excursion Range in Strength Training: Implications for Performance and Injury Prevention* (2025–2028).

EXCURSE examines how the muscle lengths at which strength training is performed shape subsequent adaptation. We compare different muscle excursion ranges and analyse their effects on muscle architecture, strength, neuromuscular activation, and mechanical properties. The aim is to determine whether looking at exercise from the perspective of the muscle, rather than only through joint motion, allows us to explain these adaptations more clearly.

This is the research line I am currently building, and we are looking for doctoral researchers to join it. [Find out more](phd.qmd).

## How we measure it

This line examines the extent to which field tests can replace or complement laboratory protocols.

My work includes validating functional threshold power, predicting VO~2~max from short tests, updating the Allen and Coggan equation, and studying anthropometric measures and muscle stiffness in road cycling.

The question is whether a test that can be used under real-world conditions tells us what we need to know—and where it stops doing so. This is my most applied research line.

*Main collaborators: Sebastian Sitko and Isaac López-Laval (Universidad de Zaragoza).*

## How the body responds

This line originated in my doctoral thesis and examines the response of cardiac biomarkers to exercise, particularly in children and adolescents.

I have been especially interested in modelling their time course: not only the value we observe, but how it evolves in the hours after exercise. This helps contextualise physiological responses that may resemble clinically concerning findings.

It is the most established of the three lines and the source of many of the methodological questions that continue to guide my research, although it now plays a more limited role in my current work.

*Main collaborators: Keith George (Liverpool John Moores University), Alejandro Legaz-Arrese (Universidad de Zaragoza), and Luis Enrique Carranza-García (Universidad Autónoma de Nuevo León).*

## The method underneath

Applied biostatistics is not a fourth research line: it is the perspective from which I approach the other three.

I am fascinated by the Bayesian paradigm because it forces us to make explicit what we assume, what we learn from the data, and how much uncertainty remains. I am particularly interested in building models that respect the actual structure of a problem: repeated measurements, time series, between-person variability, and responses that are rarely as tidy as we would like them to be.

I work with mixed-effects models, Bayesian regression, systematic reviews, and meta-analysis. I am not interested in applying the most conventional model by default, but in finding the one that best represents the process we are trying to understand. Sometimes this means leaving familiar recipes behind, testing new structures, and accepting that a more honest answer may also be a less comfortable one.

For me, statistics does not arrive at the end of a study to decide whether a result is significant. It begins much earlier: it helps formulate the question, design the study, and establish what we will be able to conclude once the data arrive.
